title: Quic ERR_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT with haproxy 3.2.x
body:
### Detailed Description of the Problem

When doing a curl with enforce http3 support, sometimes the connection just hangs and ends in `ERR_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT`. It only happens every 10-20 tries.

### Expected Behavior

Curl works every time.

### Steps to Reproduce the Behavior

Run curl multiple times like this:
```
curl -o/dev/null -v --http3-only https://<redacted-host> -I --resolve <redacted-host>:443:\[2001:678:ed0:ff00::3\]
curl -o/dev/null -v --http3-only https://<redacted-host> -I -4 --resolve <redacted-host>:443:185.150.99.3
```

### Do you have any idea what may have caused this?

_No response_

### Do you have an idea how to solve the issue?

_No response_

### What is your configuration?


https://github.com/freifunkMUC/ffmuc-salt-public/blob/main/haproxy/haproxy.cfg

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
I have not taken very much time to read all the comments here. Perhaps I have missed something. This issue really looks like the one fixed by this patch:

```
commit d753f24096dafdef227fe66621513086c2c663c1
Author: <redacted-name>
Date:   Wed Aug 27 14:18:25 2025 +0200

    BUG/MINOR: quic: reorder fragmented RX CRYPTO frames by their offsets
    
    This issue impacts the QUIC listeners. It is the same as the one fixed by this
    commit:
    
            BUG/MINOR: quic: repeat packet parsing to deal with fragmented CRYPTO
    
    As chrome, ngtcp2 client decided to fragment its CRYPTO frames but in a much
    more agressive way. This could be fixed with a list local to qc_parse_pkt_frms()
    to please chrome thanks to the commit above. But this is not sufficient for
    ngtcp2 which often splits its ClientHello message into more than 10 fragments
    with very small ones. This leads the packet parser to interrupt the CRYPTO frames
    parsing due to the ncbuf gap size limit.
    
    To fix this, this patch approximatively proceeds the same way but with an
    ebtree to reorder the CRYPTO by their offsets. These frames are directly
    inserted into a local ebtree. Then this ebtree is reused to provide the
    reordered CRYPTO data to the underlying ncbuf (non contiguous buffer). This way
    there are very few less chances for the ncbufs used to store CRYPTO data
    to reach a too much fragmented state.
    
    Must be backported as far as 2.6.
```

The problem mentioned above arrived with ngtcp2 lib which began to split and mix its CRYPTO data into several frames by packet. The issue was supposed to be solved using an ebtree to store and reorder these frames by their offsets (by packet) before providing the CRYPTO data to the TLS stack thanks to a non contiguous buffer. ngtcp does this more aggressively than chrome. Before an ebtree, a list was used. This was sufficient to fix the issue with chrome as client.

I have also noted from the tcpdump traces that the curl sends more than one Initial packet. Perhaps the issue happens when the packets are not treated in the right order (by their packet number) leading to a ncbuf fragmented state which cannot be handled. A fix could be to use an ncbuf by packet.

Given that I seem to be seeing crypto frames of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 bytes in this trace, my understanding is that we've reached the limitations of the current ncbuf design (it was meant to deal with reasonable sizes, e.g. small packets, not creating single-byte holes). The only approach I'm seeing here is to switch the ncbuf design to a bitmap, and reserve 11% of the size for the bitmap. It doesn't look dramatic though, and could possibly even simplify the logic. I just don't know how this may affect performance. In the worst case it would require to read/write 11% extra data into memory to update the map (basically writing 0xFF when filling, and 0x00 when emptying).

Given the number of occurrences of these calls, it doesn't seem too difficult to experiment with:
```
     12 ncb_is_null(

```
The issue would be more to decide whether or not to backport this at once as it would be a sensible change!

@participant2 what I meant is that this issue may happen only and only if the client is built against ngtcp2 and if **it needs to send more than one packet to send its Initial CRYPTO data**. This is not common. Most of the time, a QUIC client sends only one packet to initiate the connection. So I did not want to say that the bug fix I have mentioned could fix this new issue. It could fix it only if the client sends only one packet with Initial CRYPTO data: its role is to provide the CRYPTO data to the ncbuf() in the right order thanks to the ebtree. This never fails.

This is confirmed by the QUIC traces attached to this issue (quic-trace.txt) I have noticed lately only now. The size of the CRYPTO data depends on the TLS stack and how it is configured for the connection. According to the QUIC traces, the CRYPTO data could be added to the ncbuf for the first packet but with at least a hole at 139 offset. This is when haproxy receives the second packet that the problems arise.

During the interop tests, ngtcp2 never sends two Initial packets. This is also the case on the command line. I think that this issue should be reproducible with the correct TLS stack. My recent ngtcp2 client is built againt OpenSSL 3.5.0. According to Willy, OpenSSL 3.5.2 generates more CRYPTO data for the client. Not sure this is normal at all.

So, If we can add all the CRYPTO data to an ncbuf by packet, this could be sufficient to fix this issue. Not sure this is easy to do.

comments.author: participant7
comments.body:
Just for the record, chrome seems to be the first one to implement fragmented CRYPTO frames, a feature labelled as "Chaos protection".

https://<redacted-host>/quiche/+/cb6b51054274cb2c939264faf34a1776e0a5bab7

We already experienced issues when confronting haproxy to it and refine CRYPTO algo parsing multiple times to handle this, which seems to be enough at the time.

However, now ngtcp2 also implements a similar chaos protection.
```
commit 89c29fd8611d5e6d2f6b1f475c5e3494c376028c
Author: <redacted-name>
Date:   Mon Aug 4 22:48:06 2025 +0900

    Crumble Client Initial CRYPTO (aka chaos protection)
```

It seems to be even more aggressive than chrome, which causes haproxy to suffer again from CRYPTO frame parsing error due to the internal limitation of our owned non contiguous buffer storage type. Thus, I'm working since this week on a new buffer implementation to definitely get rid of this internal limitation, so that haproxy is able to buffer any CRYPTO frames even under extreme fragmentation conditions.
